name: The Garden of Earthly Delights (1500)
teaser: Hieronymus Bosch's triptych begins in Eden, swells into a surreal paradise crowded with naked figures and giant fruit, and ends in a black hell of instruments and torments. Nobody agrees on what it means.

exploreAction.targetName: The Garden of Earthly Delights (1500) by Bosch, center panel
exploreAction.instruction: Work left to right and resist reading it as a simple warning. Notice the oversized fruit, the glass domes, and the animals acting like people. Every object rewards a second look — the panel is a library of symbols with no index.

name: The Birth of Venus (1486)
teaser: Botticelli's Venus arrives on a shell, blown by wind gods and greeted by a handmaiden with a cloak. It was the first large-scale Renaissance painting of a nude Venus — pagan beauty made respectable by allegory.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birth of Venus (1486) by Botticelli, Uffizi
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Venus's pose — her weight on one leg, hands covering, hair long enough to reach the ground. Her body is idealized, elongated, and impossible: her neck and arms stretch beyond anatomy. That's the point — she is not a woman, she is an idea of beauty.

name: Dogs Playing Poker (1903)
teaser: Cassius Marcellus Coolidge's series of dogs around a card table became the most famous 'bad art' in America — and secretly a technical triumph of painting nine distinct canine personalities in one scene.

exploreAction.targetName: Dogs Playing Poker (1903) by Coolidge — 'A Friend in Need'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at each dog's face — the one slipping a card under the table, the one smoking a cigar, the one glaring. The jokes work because every dog has a distinct 'tell'. This is the most recognizable poker painting in history for a reason.

name: The Peacock Skirt (1893)
teaser: Aubrey Beardsley's sinuous black-and-white drawing of Salome in a peacock-patterned gown — an illustration for Oscar Wilde's play that scandalized Victorian England with its erotic decadence.

exploreAction.instruction: Look at how much is suggested with so little — the dress's eye-feathers, the figure's elongated neck, the halo-like headdress. Beardsley worked in pure black and white, and every empty space is as deliberate as every line.

name: Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871)
teaser: Whistler's portrait of his mother — he called it an 'arrangement', an experiment in color, not a portrait of a person. The Royal Academy hung it as 'Whistler's Mother', a title he hated, and it became one of the most parodied images in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Arrangement in Grey and Black (1871) by Whistler, Musée d'Orsay
exploreAction.instruction: Notice the composition: the mother is a flat silhouette against a patterned wall, her profile facing left, one foot on a stool. The frame is part of the artwork — Whistler designed it. Her hands, folded, hold a white handkerchief that is the brightest thing in the painting.

name: No. 5, 1948 (1948)
teaser: Jackson Pollock's most famous drip painting — eight feet of tangled black, gray, and brown skeins, the most expensive painting ever sold at the time ($140 million in 2006). Pollock painted it on the floor, from all sides, at the peak of his 'drip period'.

exploreAction.instruction: Don't look for a subject — look for rhythm. Follow one black line through the tangle; it loops, crosses, returns. The painting has a center of gravity near the top, where the paint is thickest. Pollock said he was 'in' the painting while he worked: it is a record of movement, not a picture.
